title: The Fool
description:
"Life is not a problem to be solved, but a reality to be lived."
Buddha

The world, as the ever-repeating circus of life, grants us an understanding of this ring: wild animals and their tamers, spectators and acrobats, clowns and jesters. In this vanity fair there is room for everyone.

With the Fool we reach the end of the Tarot's cycle. The Fool is at once beginning and end. He may be placed either at the close of the twenty-one-card series of the Major Arcana, or as its opening, right before the Magician, the sorcerer. The Fool closes one cycle and opens another. That is why the number that corresponds to him is zero, symbolized by the circle. He serves as the turning point between the lower and higher levels on the spiral of realization.

The number zero also contains all other numbers. Though it has no value in itself, zero accompanies every other number and raises its worth. It is like the Fool, who embodies the knowledge of all the other cards yet is himself utterly without value. He is the sage who is able to become a child again. He is like the innocent, simple Parsifal who, nonetheless — or perhaps precisely because of his simplicity — found the Holy Grail. The Fool is like the Wandering Jew, leading humanity forward from one cycle to the next along the spiral of life. But he is also a child, a sexless being, because he (or rather "it") has not yet separated from the primal unity. Later the child will decide whether to become the Magician or the High Priestess.

Yet the Fool is also the sage who embodies all the experience accumulated by the end of the previous cycle. Over the course of the cycle he has met and overcome all his fears, until nothing remained but himself. Death, the ultimate fear, no longer holds any meaning for him. He sees that his body is nothing more than a garment which, one fine day, he must take off and exchange for another. He knows everything and has understood everything, which is why he is able to laugh; or perhaps he knows nothing and has understood nothing, which is why he is able to laugh.

In many classic Tarot decks the Fool is shown carrying a bundle said to contain the four stages of Indian wisdom (jungle, forest, garden and house) that leads to the highest truth. He has passed through the world's dark jungle, found the first ray of light in the forest, the bright illumination in the garden, and now, at last, can rest at home. One fine day, after one more turn of the Wheel of Fortune and one more plane, he will again find a table set before him. On it he will find the four elements waiting for him, and once more he will dare to enter a new beginning as the Magician.

Placed here at the start of the game, the Fool embodies unconscious consciousness; he has not yet become aware of his own consciousness. He must pass through twenty-one stages of the Tarot, and at the end of his journey he will, at last, attain conscious consciousness. Only then will he be able to understand that the whole world dwells within his own thoughts. His world is identified with his own thoughts, and he comes to understand that everything he sees and hears is nothing other than his own projections. Herein lies the root of the Indian wisdom that teaches that the world in which we live is an illusion (maya). If a person is able to recognize the surrounding world as an illusion (a mirage), he can also transcend that illusion. If, while dreaming, we can realize that we are dreaming, then we stand on the threshold of leaving the dream and on the verge of awakening. The world is a projection, a dream; God is the only reality.

The Tarot of the Aquarian Age depicts the Fool as a two-faced figure. The left side of his face embodies the masculine aspect: smiling, knowing and indifferent, it embodies chaos, where there is room enough for everything within one vast chaotic unity. A crocodile, captured in the act of swallowing a live tiger, forms the cap that crowns the masculine half of the Fool's face. The tiger and the crocodile are sacred animals, but at the same time they symbolize animal tendencies. The other half of the Fool's face shows a beautiful woman, likewise laughing and knowing, who embodies freedom and the principle of order. Her cap is a whimsical weave of exquisite feathers. The Fool is at once she and he, chaos and wisdom, beginning and end.

This card belongs to the first letter of the Hebrew alphabet, ALEPH. ALEPH denotes the head of an ox. Why not the whole ox? Because only the head has been born. The rest of the ox remains in another dimension, in the unmanifest world. The second important feature of ALEPH is that this letter can be seen and read, but it cannot be spoken aloud. ALEPH is the beginning of unity.

The rune WUNJO means bliss, joy and pleasure. It embodies generosity, just as the Fool is the father of merriment.

The astrological sign corresponding to this card is Uranus. Uranus is the planet of intuition, spontaneity, inventiveness and originality. Uranus embodies a new sense which is, to this day, one of the most perfected of senses: intuition. This new sense marks the beginning of a new age. Only with the emergence of this new sense — with the birth of intuition — can the essence of the Age of Aquarius truly be embodied.

title: The Magician
description:
"Talent works, genius creates."
Robert Schumann

In the beginning was the word, the unborn word. Then the word was born. Before its birth the word was silence; then came the first spark of life, the divine "One," the first breath, the first thought. The Divine was the first being, the father and mother of all the numbers that followed.

If we regard the Tarot as a card game, then the Magician is the first card in the game. Or, if we see the Tarot as a means to self-knowledge, he can be regarded as the first step on the path of spiritual evolution.

The Magician embodies creative activity in the realm of ideas. He is the expression of thinking man and woman who have, for the first time, become aware of their cosmic origin.

The Magician expresses his own thoughts; he no longer acts merely as a created being, but conducts himself as a human being who has reached the level of conscious existence. Until this moment he was a tangle of feelings and emotions, and his life was devoted chiefly to satisfying material needs — material hunger had to be satisfied, sexual need demanded satisfaction, and its resolution contented him only insofar as (and if) he ever looked beyond his own life. Only in this way, it seemed to him, could he project himself into life after death. He is influenced by his surroundings, his parents manipulate him, his upbringing has shaped him; thus he forgets his divine origin. His awakening as the Magician gives him the chance for a sudden return to his cosmic home. He begins to make conscious efforts, so that through a process of inner evolution he may find the way back home. His way home may be long and exhausting, or, alternatively, easy and joyful: it depends on whether or not he can develop the necessary qualities within himself. The twenty-two cards of the Major Arcana shed light upon this path, so that he may more easily find his way home.

The Magician embodies the beginning of a new idea, a new state, a new work or activity, as well as a playful possession of material things. He knows and governs the four elements: fire, water, air and earth. He passes through the first trial — the trial by fire — on the path of initiation, and receives the magic wand. Through his striving to discover the truth, he conquers the realm of air and receives the sword of truth. When he opens his understanding of the earth, he is given the gift of coins (disks). In the end, he is allowed to drink from the cup of wisdom.

The Magician stands under the sign of Mercury (or Hermes in Greek mythology). People saw in him the patron of trade and exchange. Hermes is marked by sociability, flexibility and congeniality, qualities with which the Magician is likewise endowed.

In the winged Hermes (the word "herme" means "waymark") the Greeks saw a signpost. For them he was the god of the road for all wanderers, who accompanied their souls on the way to the Underworld. In this light, the Magician is a guide through all the stages of the game of Tarot, which is not necessarily a journey to the Underworld, but into our own world and to our own center. Hermes, messenger of the gods, embodies speed, intelligence and curiosity, but also a certain inclination toward intrigue and power.

This card, like all the others in the Major Arcana of the Tarot of the Aquarian Age, is associated with a number and a letter: a letter of the Hebrew alphabet on the left, and a rune on the right. Both of these symbols express the meaning of the card.

The Magician is often (also outside the Tarot of the Aquarian Age deck) assigned the letter ALEPH, the first letter of the Hebrew alphabet, which corresponds to his divine aspect and to silence. The primal sound has not yet been spoken. The bursting-forth of this first sound breaks the silence, and BETH (house) arises. BETH is the second letter of the alphabet, and we find it on the left side of the Magician's card. BETH is our home, this manifest world as against the unmanifest world beyond it — which at the same time reminds us that it exists.

In the right corner of the card is the rune FEHU, which means "cattle," and therefore, indirectly, symbolizes wealth or the mystery of gold. FEHU also signifies fire and energy. The power of FEHU lies in the hands of the truly noble. It must remain under the control of those responsible enough to use this power wisely. Anyone who abuses this power should beware, because sooner or later the energy that has been transformed into its negative expression will boomerang back upon whoever wielded it.

The Magician holds this power in his hands; everything depends on his choice. Will he decide to become an evil or a good magician? He stands at the beginning of his path, and every subsequent phase (every card) requires him to make a decision.

title: The High Priestess
description:
"All true greatness is born of stillness."
Thomas Carlyle

The High Priestess is card number two, the card of male/female polarity, of separation from unity and the attainment of duality. Only by passing through the duality of father and mother can one arrive at the phenomenon of triunity. In the Magician, unity rules: he is the masculine source, activity and beginning. The High Priestess embodies the opposite pole: she is the embodiment of femininity and its transcending aspect. Everything about her image speaks of acceptance, receptivity, stillness and a wisdom that comes from within. It is not without reason that this card is placed under the sign of the Moon, whose image suggests feminine sensitivity — the lunar aspect.

In the Tarot of the Aquarian Age the High Priestess is depicted with closed eyes, because feelings come first for her. She has no need to open her eyes, because she is already well acquainted with the world of maya (illusion). She knows that reality lies only in her inner world — everything else is merely a projection of her craving mind.

Her card corresponds to two dimensions: this world and the beyond, day and night, light and darkness, and thus to all the pairs of polar aspects we encounter in our life: warm/cold, beautiful/ugly, god/devil, and so on. Without one side, we could never understand the other. Everything that forms unity in the Magician now, as a continuation of its search, divides itself into opposites, so that it may experience itself through its opposite.

The man and woman who stand at the stage of the Magician have resolved their existential problems in a more or less satisfactory way. But when they move into the phase of the High Priestess, they begin to suspect that another reality awaits them, one that lies beyond so-called "reality." They set off on an inner journey, lifting a corner of the veil of the High Priestess, Isis, who raises her veil and reveals her secret to the true seeker.

This second figure of the Major Arcana signifies intuition, harmony, wisdom on the spiritual plane, authority, benevolence, guidance, a moral or religious path, calm and silence.

The letter of the Hebrew alphabet in the left corner of the card, GIMEL, means camel — the camel that will carry us on its back across the desert of our imagination's dreams until we reach the oasis that will be our true home.

The rune URUZ (aurochs) symbolizes the strength needed to give form. URUZ, as the mother of manifestation, points us toward the path of creation and, thus, at the same time toward the next card — the Empress.

title: The Empress
description:
"He who rests upon the stillness of his heart, acknowledging it as his authority — what other authority could he need?"
Zhuangzi

From the two preceding cards, the Magician (the masculine source, active energy) and the High Priestess (the feminine source, receptive energy), arises the third card, the Empress, who symbolizes the child, the created world, the visible universe and nature. This third card emerges from the union of opposites, through which something new is born — the child, the "three." The energetic quality of the third card differs quite considerably from that of its predecessors. In the second card we saw woman in her mystical, contemplative aspect; in the third card we meet a young, defiant woman who confidently displays her femininity. She radiates a thirst for life; a haughty sensuality sparkles in her eyes. The crown on her head signifies consciousness. She is fully aware of her power and her attractiveness as a woman.

The masculine source, paying her due homage, brings her his seed as an offering, from which new life may arise. In this way the eternal cycles of nature move through birth, life and death. The Empress is the patroness of all three aspects. She guards the great mystery of conception, as well as the mystery of pregnancy. The fertility and abundance with which she surrounds herself grant us spring, the season of rebirth, when everything is fresh and young, only to become dry and old by autumn. She is Persephone, daughter of Demeter, who spends half of every year (the winter months) in the Underworld, and the other six months (summer) upon the surface of the earth.

Fire is the element corresponding to both this card and the Magician. The Empress's burning red hair and the recklessly bold, penetrating expression of her eyes underscore her closeness to fire. Like the Magician, she embodies activity. Her symbol is Venus, goddess of love. Because of Venus's alluring femininity, offerings were brought to her altar.

The Empress also embodies the Great Mother, the primal ancestress from whom all that is material descended. She holds within her three manifestations of God: creation, preservation and destruction. She represents the three dimensions of space: depth, width and height. She symbolizes the three phases of life: birth, life and death. The laws of matter rule on Earth, and everything that has been born must also die.

People who have reached this phase understand that Mother Nature will lead, protect and preserve them on their earthly path. This explains why they begin to care for their bodies, which give them the chance to experience this thing called "life." From this moment on they will begin to pay conscious attention to their health, so that the outer, material shell may serve them for as long as possible, until it finally returns to Mother Earth.

The card of the Empress signifies energy, activity, evolution, success, abundance, initiative and will. Together with her creative nature, the Empress participates in the very act of creation.

The Hebrew letter of this card is DALETH (door). The path of life leads to this door, in order to show us the diversity and abundance that lies beyond ourselves. After passing through this door we, in the end, pass through further gates, as we once again begin a new life.

To the third card belongs the rune THURISAZ (thorn and/or thunder). THURISAZ embodies the potential energy contained within all bipolar extremes. The power of rebirth and fertility fulfills itself through the mystery of the rune THURISAZ.

title: The Emperor
description:
"Too many rulers are never a blessing for the people; only one should rule one kingdom alone."
Homer

After the Empress comes the Emperor, who continues her work. If the third card symbolizes creation, the Emperor arrives in order to bring order into that creation. He draws boundaries where they are needed. He shapes and gives form, and rules the material world with wisdom, understanding and love. In the Major Arcana of the Tarot of the Aquarian Age, this fourth card depicts a man in the prime of his life. His face is turned to the east, toward the source of the sun and of the new. He is open to new teachings or new currents, which he can work with and test before passing them on to his people. The hermetic ideogram of the lily (fleur-de-lis) in the right corner is the symbol that best expresses the nobility of his soul. It shows that a true ruler must avoid persecution, primitive imperialism and self-worship, and instead rule with heart, wisdom and reason.

The fourth arcanum is the card of matter. The Emperor knows that his soul is enclosed within matter, and he believes that discipline, order and force of will can set it free. This is an example of how he wishes to accomplish what he has conceived. But since he knows how difficult it is to always make wise and correct decisions, he is also full of love and compassion for others who have not yet reached the same progress as he has.

In the course of his journey along this path to himself, the Emperor has become strict and unyielding, almost harsh. But the inner fire of faith, which inspires him, also allows him to understand that nothing is fixed, that everything is "becoming" in an endless process of transformation. Even his temporary status as Emperor will change, when in the next phase of the process he too must become wiser and more mature.

When you met him earlier, at the stage of the Magician, he was still inexperienced, curious and full of eagerness to accomplish great deeds. Now we meet him again in the phase of the Emperor, where he has become a mature, enlightened and knowledgeable ruler. People who have reached this stage have gained mastery over their bodies. They seek an awakened love within themselves, so as to freely give this love to themselves and to those around them. They respect and establish boundaries; they protect and are protected from above. They give birth to new ideas and thoughts and give them form (matter). Intuitively sensing the power that flows from their thoughts, they have begun to discipline their minds, though they do not yet know the secret of "right thinking" — they will attain that knowledge later.

The fourth card stands under the sign of Aries, which signifies fire, persistence and courage. The astrological ram is ruled by Mars, the god of war. A good Emperor must understand this force in order to transform it from a destructive power into a creative, stable energy.

The Hebrew letter HE (window) adorns the fourth card. A house has a door and a window, through which the Emperor can engage with the outer world, with other points of view and other ideas. The Emperor need only close the door and window again to restore the separation, isolation and solitude that he sometimes needs. When he has once more replenished his inner energy, he can throw the window open again.

The rune ANSUZ symbolizes the royal stag and Izir, a young god of Norse mythology; ANSUZ also embodies skillfulness and skillful speech, the eloquence with which the emperor speaks to his people.

The Emperor represents the highest achievement on the plane of power and ego. This understanding comes to all who have reached this stage, along with the authority and maturity required for their next step on the path.

title: The Hierophant
description:
"Wisdom lies only in wisdom."
Goethe

Just as the Emperor continues the work of the Empress, the Priest completes the work begun by the High Priestess. The High Priestess keeps her wisdom to herself. Now, the fifth card, the sage, is ready to help and guide the people who seek him. The wisdom that has grown through personal effort has raised him into the cosmic sphere, and now he stands in direct contact with reality.

He tested his skill as the Magician, developed new abilities as the High Priestess, established a bond with nature as the Empress, passed through matter as the Emperor — now he perfects his spirit as the Priest.

In many typical Tarot decks, the Priest is shown seated between two columns. Two figures kneel before him. The figure on the right, bowed, in a contracted posture, symbolizes the dogmatic path to religion. This type of person still lives according to the exoteric aspect of religion, and is grounded in dogma. The mission of established churches ought to lead such people toward independence, rather than making them dependent or allowing them to languish in their dependency. But if churches truly fulfilled this task, they would have to give up a portion of their power.

The kneeling figure on the left, upright yet still in a posture of reverence, symbolizes the independent path to religion. This figure embodies people who consciously seek their own path to God, people who know that liberation given by any external source will bring little benefit. They must free themselves, which is far more difficult, because it demands a love for oneself that must be developed from within, by themselves alone. How else could we love our neighbors as ourselves?

The number five corresponds to the fourfold unity fertilized by the One, who is born of the cosmic dimension. Five is transcended matter, guided by spirit. In the Tarot of the Aquarian Age this is remarkably depicted in the figure of a wise old man. Only the lower part of his face is clearly visible. His forehead, the sphere of thought, is invisible, yet evidently filled with cosmic energy.

The Priest signifies a spiritual master, an initiate, a seeker or a source of counsel, initiation and transformation. People who have reached this level of understanding are no longer helpless before the power of their carnal instincts. Many people come to them for advice, which they give from a position of benevolent authority and good will.

The symbol of Taurus, the bull, is found on the right side of the card. This bull embodies masculine energy and sexuality. It is ruled by Venus, who embodies femininity. This means that the masculine and feminine sources are united, and polarity has been transcended. A parallel can be drawn between this card and the second card (the High Priestess), which draws its meaning and power from polarity. This polarity has been dissolved in the fifth card, the Priest, who unites both energies — masculine and feminine — within himself. Only in this way can he consciously establish contact with another dimension.

The Hebrew letter VAV means a hook, a connecting line, something that joins two separate things together. Man has become a synthesis of man and woman, a hermaphrodite, joined from above. The striving of the lower toward the higher, as well as the receiving of the lower from the higher, strengthens this connection.

The rune RAIDHO means riding (on horseback), a wheel or a cart — transport on the path of cosmic energy. But we are still at the beginning of the path. Neither our horse nor our cart can remain motionless. The Priest still has many obstacles to overcome on the way to the final goal.

title: The Lovers
description:
"You want to be loved because you do not love yourself, but as you begin to love yourself, you stop asking whether someone else loves you or not."
Krishnamurti

The first five arcana of the Tarot represent five philosophical principles that guide us along the spiritual path. The sixth card gives us the opportunity to practice what they have taught.

Is there anything in the whole world more majestic and more beautiful than to love and to be loved? Through love the individual moves from I to Thou and into the union of We. Love means to open oneself, to give oneself, to fuse together into unity, to dissolve into the other and thus find salvation together. In many rites existing in archaic traditions, sexuality was elevated to the level of a high art and regarded as the key to higher consciousness. It still offers the only opportunity for ordinary beings to act in the image and likeness of their creator, since in the act of creation we ourselves become creators of new life. That is why the bodily act of love has parallels with another act on a higher plane.

The energy that flows from I to Thou overshadows the ego, which fades against the backdrop of this energy. Although the ego still exists, it has yielded the central position, placing Thou at the center.

The sixth card in the Tarot of the Aquarian Age depicts two young people embracing one another. Estranged from themselves, each is in intimate closeness with the other, sharing the lightness of ecstasy. Their faces are peaceful and relaxed, their postures express tenderness and gratitude. Two opposites, united in a single embrace, have found each other. Now they dream the dream of love together.

Adam has found Eve. Their love is not a sin, but it would be a sin for them to be ashamed of their sexuality. Such shame would be like a second expulsion from paradise. A new entry into this paradise lays bare all that is free of false modesty and imposed ethical norms, attains self-realization, and is nourished by a living morality, a source that lies within each of us.

The two figures on the sixth card are naked. Nakedness in the Tarot always means that human beings are showing themselves as they are, with all their desires and aspirations. Having shed the false feeling of shame, they will become as they were in the beginning, before they tasted the fruit of the Tree of Knowledge.

If we look closely at the card, we can make out two separate planes. The lower position holds the faces of the Lovers and belongs to the worldly, to the material world. The upper position encloses the bodies of the Lovers and belongs to the cosmic, spiritual world. People who have reached this stage can decide for themselves which world they wish to belong to.

In many typical Tarot decks this card is called "The Crossroads," because diverging paths are associated with sexuality and decision-making. This defining decision is represented in the image of a young man standing between two women, unable to choose between them. One woman expresses virtue, the other vice. People at this stage of development often find themselves in a dramatic situation, running into conflicts and dilemmas over a decision still to be made. This may involve a choice between two professions, two paths, two women or two men; in any case we must use everything we have learned so far. The act of deciding does not matter in itself; what matters is that we learn to decide from an ethical and moral standpoint. Nor does the outcome of the decision matter very much, since our decision will correspond to our abilities and to what we have learned. When we consider that the human being has been endowed with the power to exercise free choice, and can therefore reach God, we (like every adult initiate) will undoubtedly apply this power to the greatest possible benefit. And besides, there are no wrong decisions, since any and every decision, in the end, favors the process of a person's maturing. God is beyond time; He awaits us in His eternal love.

The sixth card is endowed with two aspects. It is the card of Thou, of a decision about something that lies outside yourself. It is also the card of the Beloved, of harmony, exchange, feeling, and at the same time the card of the unease that precedes a difficult choice.

The Hebrew letter ZAYIN (weapon) tells us that initiates at this stage of evolution must use all their weapons (everything they have been taught), so as not to lose the awareness of unity they achieved and which they feel within themselves at the stage of the Priest. According to the law of opposites, the gate through which they experience love also opens hatred within them, and they will need their weapons in order to defend themselves against that hatred.

The rune KENAZ (torch) embodies the deep connection between sexuality and creativity. It signifies passion and a thirst for love, but also difficulty, sacrifice, and that which attracts.

The card of the Lovers is associated with Gemini, the pair. Mercury, who rules the Magician, also governs Gemini and thus change, movement and information. The element of the twins is air, the mediator that carries thoughts, sighs and vows of love from one lover to the other. The souls of the twins meet each other within a deep, inexhaustible and unbreakable eternal atmosphere that belongs to the Lovers alone.

The sixth card speaks to us from the cosmic plane. But if we wish to learn the lessons of life, we must also descend to the plane of earth; we must become acquainted with physical love. And we must also learn to decide and to make difficult choices. The Magician, on his evolutionary path, must learn whether to use what he has experienced solely for his own good, or for the good of all humanity. Only by sensing his own self-identification can he develop further, as we see on the next card (the Chariot).

title: The Chariot
description:
"The new forces its way inward by force."
Friedrich Nietzsche

The Chariot forms the conclusion of the first cycle of spiritual evolution and, at the same time, the beginning of the next. The Magician, in the phase of the Lovers, has passed his trial. He has learned love, and how to make right decisions. Now, at the stage of the Chariot, he must put his newfound independence into practice.

Card number seven of the Tarot of the Aquarian Age depicts this situation in a strikingly modern image. It shows a young man in a race car. In what art is he practicing? Naturally, he is pursuing his own inner balance and the balance of his vehicle. He needs absolute concentration in order to win the race, which means he must remain perfectly centered. The positive and negative energies that form the basis of every person must vibrate in harmony. He must possess perfect mastery over his body, and his thoughts must be so concentrated that his desires and aspirations lead him to his goal. All of this endows him with an extraordinarily strong capacity for self-assertion. He possesses the power to overcome every obstacle. His helmet recalls the helmets of the knights who fought in medieval tournaments. It protects him from destructive impressions that could potentially weaken his will. He wants to reach the goal, he wants to win, and he will win. Nothing and no one can prevent him from taking first place in the race of his life.

This is the first card that shows how the ego builds its relationships with others. We already saw the I-Thou aspect in the sixth card (the Lovers); now in the seventh card (the Chariot), the aspect of I is reflected at the level of the ego, sensing itself as opposed to others. The rider is manly and strong; his will leads him wherever he wants to go. His Chariot, which embodies his energies, carries him from triumph to triumph. He was born to win. The man and woman at this stage are young people separating themselves from their parents' home in order to learn about life on their own. They are full of ambition and a striving for freedom, seeking their place in society. In the phase represented by this card, human beings learn to direct their energies in order to achieve a breakthrough on the material plane. Later, they will be able to apply that same power again in order to enter the spiritual world.

The rider needs all his skill and courage in order to reach the goal he has set for himself. Even though Death constantly accompanies him in every race, he is not afraid. Every true hero incorporates the aspect of death into his life. With every battle he wins, he becomes more and more certain that he will triumph over Death. The price of victory is his own life. Understood in this way, everything he does advances his evolution.

In the left corner of the card we find the letter CHETH (fence). People close the windows and doors of their homes and even build a fence around their property. This means that people in this phase are concentrated exclusively on themselves, avoiding all outside influence.

The rune of this card is HAGALAZ (hailstone). HAGALAZ is a code, or pattern, of becoming and completion.

The Chariot is associated with the sign of Cancer, a water sign. Because of its penetrating, gentle qualities, water is often stronger and more enduring than all the other elements. This means that the Rider is subject to his feelings, guided by the subconscious (which the crab symbolizes).

The seventh card expresses masculinity, intellect, creative power. On the next card we will meet this same energy in its feminine aspect.

title: Strength
description:
"If you can simply observe what you are and remain flexible, you will discover that you can develop endlessly."
Krishnamurti

The Rider of the seventh card has learned the lessons of self-confidence, self-assertion and courage. Now we meet Strength in the image of a woman. The eighth card of the Tarot of the Aquarian Age depicts a young woman in the throes of an ecstatic, passionate surrender. Everything about her expresses the sensuality and pleasure she feels through being within her own body. Experiencing and giving herself with her whole heart, she embodies Shakti, the divine consort of Shiva, who gives strength to her husband through her tantric, sexual union. She is also the saint who gives herself to her divine beloved in mystical union.

The lion in the foreground symbolizes the lower instincts of the human being: suppressed sexuality, envy, hatred, jealousy, the desire for money, the thirst for power. But this woman has tamed her lion; now he lies at her feet and seems almost to smile at the fact that a frail woman has succeeded in taming him. The strength this woman possesses is the irresistible power of love. Even though she does not fight, she subdues; without conquest. Yet she is the victor, and without oppressing, she nonetheless transforms.

Herein lies our great task: not to suppress the lower energies within a person, but to transform them. The truly wise woman and man know that every power available to them can only continue to serve them if they use it wisely. Everything that is lower must be raised, so that it can become exalted. In this way, negative energies too can work together with positive energies to achieve the "great task."

The woman on this card works with the same energy as the Magician. Her motto is activity, but also surrender for her own sake and for that of others. Only by feeling others as deeply as she feels herself can she be true. Love, understanding and compassion are her "weapons." When she allows her love to blossom freely, however, she often encounters prejudices, which she has tried to transform by learning to see herself in every circumstance. She communes with the lion lying at her feet, mirroring him and, through the power of love, transforming his lower instincts into strong traits of character that now enrich her whole being.

The man and woman at this stage of development feel themselves to be at the fullness of their energetic potential. The woman in this phase learns to interact with masculine energy, the man learns to work with feminine energy. In this way, both people combine their masculine and feminine aspects, in order to attain wholeness within themselves. Just as on the card of the Chariot, there is a victor here too. Having tamed the beast within, our Strength and our animal powers unite, to master whatever comes.

The astrological symbol of Leo, a fire sign, appears on the seventh card of the Major Arcana. Leo embodies energy, courage, nobility of character and fiery energy.

The Hebrew letter TETH (womb with embryo) denotes the life that rests, securely hidden within. True strength guards this energy and calls upon itself only when necessary.

The rune SOWILO (sun) signifies will, life energy, victory, glory and success — aspects that complete the card of Strength. On the next stage (the Hermit), all of this is reevaluated anew.

title: The Hermit
description:
"When a man has found peace within himself, there is no need to seek it anywhere else."
La Rochefoucauld

As you walk the path of the Tarot, the atmosphere grows ever more rarefied. The road is no longer as straight as it was on the card of the Chariot; there is no place to rest, as there was on the card of the Lovers. The ecstasy contained in the card of Strength has acquired a new face, a new dimension. The self-giving ecstasy of the eighth card has transformed, closed in upon itself and turned inward, shielding itself from the outer world, in order to become a radiant, inner truth.

What are those people seeking who have already succeeded in reaching this stage of development? They are seeking truth. They know the world in which they lived, which offered them countless manifestations of truth. But the truth they seek belongs to them. It is pure, independent of outside influence, and springs like clear water from its own inner source.

In order to reach this stage of development, seekers must withdraw, isolate themselves from other people and their opinions. The Tarot of the Aquarian Age depicts the Hermit at the center of the ninth card as a man whose penetrating gaze reveals that he has attained self-knowledge and realization. A delicate, net-like pattern adorns his face. The artist could not have found a deeper symbol than this net to express the idea that seekers in the phase of the Hermit have fenced themselves off from everything external. Their net is finally woven and, though it is not visible to everyone, it protects them like a suit of medieval chainmail, guarding their solitude so that they may remain alone with themselves.

Life in the outer world, with its endless pursuit of fame, power and money, has shown the Hermit the meaning of Death for those whose lives are based solely on materialistic values. The Hermit strives for authentic life, for the life that lies beyond death. This, as he now understands, is the only thing that can be found if one follows the spiritual path. That is why he freely joins with all those who, like him, are engaged in fulfilling the "great task." He wishes to continue learning and to affirm himself. He never overestimates his own wisdom, because he is acutely aware that much still awaits him.

He has renounced the importance of his persona, because he no longer wants to act from behind a mask. Persona is the word used to describe the masks that actors in ancient Greece held before their faces, in order to better express the roles they were playing. It was a great step forward when people could allow themselves to step out of the personas in which they so often believed unconditionally. But as long as they continue to find success wearing this persona in the theater of life, separating themselves from their masks will be a difficult task.

The Hermit has freed himself from his mask (his persona). He has isolated himself, distanced himself from society and become a "stranger." Other people no longer understand him, but he does not value their understanding very much. He has experienced the truth within himself, and it speaks the truth to the genuine seeker who penetrates the protective screen and reaches himself.

Alongside the Hermit's central face, the Tarot of the Aquarian Age card depicts him in the form of an old man. Carrying his belongings and a faintly glowing lantern, partly hidden within his long hooded cloak, he is in search of his path. The cloak symbolizes his estrangement from the world. The lantern helps him find his true way. Every step must be carefully examined and tested, but his lantern (which in this case symbolizes his knowledge and intellect) supports him, so that he need not wander lost and without hope.

In many traditional Tarot decks a small snake is shown on the ground at the Hermit's feet. It symbolizes the intuition that, at this very moment, carries with it a wonderful chance, or a misfortune, that allows the Hermit to lead himself out of the labyrinth in which he has temporarily become lost. The net on the man's face in the ninth card of the Tarot of the Aquarian Age can also be interpreted as a labyrinth, a symbol of our entanglement in our own desires and notions. Only Ariadne's thread, the snake (and thus, once again, our intuition), can free us from this self-imposed confinement.

Individuals at this stage of development feel the need to leave everything behind, to become solitary hermits. Often they do indeed isolate themselves in monasteries and ashrams. If, however, they have not yet completed the inner transformation into the Hermit, their problems will inevitably follow them, to whatever corner of the earth they may travel. On the other hand, these individuals may feel themselves to be hermits even while in the thick of worldly life. In the phase of the Hermit, human beings draw strength from their own nature, their inner sources, and know that they can always take refuge in the shelter of their inner home whenever necessary, in order to regain the strength they need for the long path of their solitary wanderings.

The Hebrew letter on the left side of the card is YOD (hand). YOD represents the child who still remained an embryo in TETH. This child has emerged from the mystery and takes fate into its own hands. During the first five years of life, children still enjoy close contact with the other world from which they came; they still know the mystery of their origin. The veil of sleep has not yet closed tightly over their eyes, so they can still joyfully reach out with natural curiosity and take into their own hands the threads that will become the patterns of their own lives.

The Hermit knows neither existential anxiety, nor vanity, nor a thirst for fame or renown. He is simply what he is, by the mere fact that "he is." In this light we can understand why true sages seek the child within themselves. They rediscover the inner child whose existence they had denied for so long, because they were embarrassed that the child would not "fit" their adult world. "Unless you become as little children," or become like the hands of a child, hands that can take hold of everything — and nothing...

The rune ISA in the right corner of the card means ice as primal matter, a source, a primal current, stillness or a period of trial. ISA is the frozen earth from which consciousness arises and carries out its own self-transformation. Sometimes, however, the path is scarcely wider than a hair, and it takes all our skill and dexterity to successfully continue our journey.

title: Wheel of Fortune
description:
"A happy man can make others happy, and if he does so, he will increase his own happiness."
Johann Ludwig Wilhelm Gleim

In every culture the Wheel has always held enormous symbolic significance. From the very earliest beginnings to the present day, whether in the context of cult, religion, or simply as a means of transport, the Wheel has served as an image of the great centrifugal force that carries within it the aspect of change and motion, and upon which humanity bases its being-in-the-world.

Centrifugal force denotes the motion arising from the kinetic energy of a physical body. But the mystery of the Wheel lies in the fact that it possesses a second force, a centripetal force, an energy directed toward the center, which maintains balance.

If a man or a woman can transform centrifugal force into centripetal force, they have grasped the chief lesson of their lives. If elementary particles strive toward the periphery of the Wheel and spin endlessly under the action of centripetal force, they have now become its central point. This means that they have become identical with the force itself, and this force is the cause of the motion. If before they were the helpless victims of their fate, now they have become its co-creators. Chronos, the god of time, personally places the key into their hands. If human beings can remain in a state of absolute concentration and stay at their own centered point of balance, then they leave the dimension of "space and time" behind and find themselves in eternity, in that state of existence from which they came and which will be their home when they shed the husk of their body.

What keeps us from consciously living in this eternity today? The obstacles are two great human tendencies that we have not yet fully mastered: the instinct of self-preservation and the instinct for the continuation of the species. Both instincts still revolve around our Wheel of Fortune. Our words, thoughts and feelings still lead us away from the center. We must learn to be entirely within ourselves, to rest at our point of balance, and let the Wheel of Samsara (the cycle of birth and death) revolve around us.

Everything personal must become impersonal. We must stop being actors in this theatrical play and simply become its spectators. We can safely entrust the role of director to the higher power, at least until we attain full understanding of the whole plot of the drama. If we have learned this lesson, we will be surprised to find that this drama has transformed into a comedy — a Divine Comedy, in which each of us plays our own, God-appointed role. From this moment on, the pain of life and the "hard blows" of fate come to an end, because we have stopped resisting, and we take part actively and joyfully in every turn of the great Wheel. We have recognized that a lesson must be drawn from every so-called problem, and we regard every new "problem" as an opportunity for further growth. Now we are no longer beings revolving around it, but have taken fate into our own hands and can actively turn the Wheel of Fortune ourselves.

This card signifies happiness, success and unexpected gain, but it also marks a period of stagnation. When it seems to us that no progress is occurring, one must wait until the Wheel begins to turn again.

Jupiter, as the principle of equilibrium and stability, is the lord of this card. KAPH (hand) is the Hebrew letter of this card. In contrast to the symbol on the ninth card, this "hand" denotes the ability to take and to embrace. From this moment on, the house of this world will be governed from another plane, and human activity will be subordinated to divine law.

The rune JERA means the solar year. It symbolizes the annual cycle, the harvest and fertility, good times and the cycle of life. It is the rune of "eternal rebirth." JERA embodies the idea of resurrection, the coming and going of existence, blossoming and withering, as manifested through the seasons. Just as all things move and turn in a circle, so too does the karmic Wheel turn with us and around us. The only chance for liberation from the eternal cycle of birth and death lies in reaching the center of one's own Wheel and living here in "eternal being."

title: Justice
description:
"Justice is the name of the cunning construction of a majestic edifice beneath the vault of heaven."
Friedrich Schiller

Justice, as its number shows, is the central card of the Tarot's Major Arcana. It occupies its rightful position at the moment when seekers have reached the central point of their evolution and have grown mature enough to judge for themselves. When they are ready to undergo this judgment, they are also ready to experience divine justice.

The spiritual lesson formed the central point of the previous card (the Wheel of Fortune). Now, on the eleventh card, the time has come to put these skills into practice.

Justice is the card of discernment. Before you can pass a verdict, you must first be able to decide. The man and woman at this stage of development have so purified their intellectual and spiritual faculties that they are capable of "standing trial" together with themselves and their surroundings. They have separated themselves from habits and friends who no longer suit them. This separation happens naturally, as the circle of their interests no longer corresponds to their former friends and company. People in the phase of Justice tend to be stricter with themselves and with others. They know that, through their deeds, they themselves are the creators of their own lives. They understand that their parents, upbringing and environment are likewise generated by their thoughts, and, consequently, they can hold no one but themselves responsible for their own life. The moment they understand these interdependencies, they take up the sword of justice in order to separate themselves from everything that binds them or hinders their further development.

Card number eleven in the Tarot of the Aquarian Age depicts Justice as a young woman with a blindfold over her eyes. Her blouse is severe, with a high collar closing tightly around her throat. She prefers not to make use of the influence of her feminine charms, though at the same time she is confident of herself and responsible for herself in her feminine aspect. She shows clearly that nothing is given to us as a gift, but she also shows that nothing is hidden from us. We ourselves are responsible for everything we receive, feel or experience.

Blind, impartial Justice holds the scales in her hand. This means that in order to decide anything, one must first try it, weigh it and consider it before a decision is made. The sword in the foreground marks this card's sign of Mars. Once the decision has been made, the sword separates what is useful from what is useless.

This aspect of weighing, of comparing physical weight or the relative qualities of immaterial things, is also contained in the polarity between the energies of Mars and Venus. It is Venus who rules Libra. The harmony of these two energies — masculine and feminine — makes it possible for us to find our own center, to be highly demanding of ourselves, and to discover a deep justice at the core of our being. Without understanding this, you cannot dare to become an instrument of divine justice.

The Hebrew letter of the eleventh card is LAMED (an ox-goad, or staff). The hand takes up the staff and defines the boundaries of human justice. Divine justice governs this hand from above. One day, human justice will once again meet divine justice, and the two will become one again.

The rune NAUTHIZ means need. Necessity, of course, is the mother of invention. As a teacher, need has always contributed to the process of evolution. Only great need can provide sufficient energy to move on to the next phase.

title: The Hanged Man
description:
"The path of salvation leads neither to the right nor to the left; it leads to your own heart, and only there is God, and only there is peace."
Hermann Hesse

The path of the Tarot leading up to card number eleven (Justice) is described as the active, virile, Dorian, or dry path. It represents the first active steps that initiates must take on their way to perfection.

Complete and absolute surrender occurs in card number twelve (the Hanged Man), and thus begins the second half of the Tarot's path. This part of the journey is described as the passive, feminine, Ionian, mystical, or moist part.

Here, the Magician, or the first card, becomes the mystic. Having passed through Justice, he is filled with the desire to become part of the divine truth. He has abandoned his search, because he understands that the search itself was the main obstacle preventing him from finding truth. He has turned inward, to such a degree that he has also turned around, been turned upside down. He surrenders to himself with absolute love for his Creator, on Whom alone he depends and wishes to depend.

From this act of surrender arises the certainty that the Creator will not abandon him, and at the same time he understands his own task. His mission is to love and encourage everyone he meets, so that they too might one day be ready to personally experience the sensations of the Hanged Man.

Card number twelve is also described as the card of Christ. It is the card of "Thy will be done," and of the complete renunciation of one's own will.

When we look at this card in the Tarot of the Aquarian Age, we see a naked young man hanging by his left leg. His right leg is free, and together with the left leg the two limbs form a cross. Both his arms are bound behind his back. His head hangs down, and his hair almost touches the water — from which, perhaps, he arose. Water in this context symbolizes the subconscious. The Hanged Man has arisen from the subconscious. He is not yet permitted to look fully into the realm of higher consciousness, but he has already touched this plane with one foot. Although his bound arms suggest that he avoids all physical activity, his mental, clairvoyant, telepathic and spiritual powers are fully activated. The sign of the cross that his legs form means that the material world no longer holds any power over him. He has stopped dreaming of "having" and begun to live the dream of "being." The Magician, at the beginning of the Tarot's path, wants to use his powers to rule; the Hanged Man, who has developed along the path of knowledge, wishes only to serve.

The young man's nakedness symbolizes his denial, his renunciation of everything superficial and material. He wants to return to his source in the very same complete nakedness in which he was brought into the world.

The young man's face shows no trace of pain or sorrow, but instead expresses a deep understanding and acceptance of his harsh trial. The sacrifice made for the sake of love, shown here, rewards him with the gift of divine love.

The astrological symbol of the card is the trident, the emblem of Neptune, the Roman god of water known to the Greeks as Poseidon. Water is the element of this card, confirmed by the Hebrew letter MEM (water) as the primal substance, the bearer of all life and the mother of the subconscious.

TIWAZ (the pole star) is the rune of this card. TIWAZ embodies the exceptional power of unattached transcendental wisdom at the center of all things.

title: Death
description:
"Every time life calls, the heart must be ready to say farewell and begin again."
Hermann Hesse

O Death! You merciful father-god, you who lead people from becoming to becoming, be welcome among us. Without you we would not recognize the precious gift of life, would not be grateful enough to accept it. You begin to accompany us with our very first breath and wait patiently for us to draw our last. Your loving service to humanity is in no way cruel; only those who do not know you, or those who cannot remember their previous encounters with you, are troubled, out of ignorance. This fear is the only true Death.

If a woman and a man cannot become mature enough to one day overcome their fear of Death, they will fall into the hands of that beautiful friend, great Change.

In many cultures death appears in the image of a woman. In all the Romance languages, for instance, the word denoting death requires a feminine article — la morte, la muerte, or la mort — and each of these words uses the same basic letters present in the word "mama" in those same languages. After all this, would you not wish for your own body to one day be lowered into the comforting, soft soil of Mother Earth?

Matter turns into mother and transcends her, while the mother herself is a materialized part of God. Through the gift of the body which, enriched by life's experience, now returns to her, she herself becomes one with its sensations. Only in this way can she transform into the father, into the union that reigns eternally.

The death of the physical body frees the spirit, which is now free to return to the source, to undergo the necessary purification and prepare itself for its next incarnation in earthly life. Together with its new birth into the material sphere and its new entry into the world of becoming, the spirit is once again accompanied by its mother (la morte).

The Tarot of the Aquarian Age reveals the aspect of life and death in a remarkable way. In the lower part of the card is depicted a human skull, out of which an angelic female body arises. This figure represents both Death and rebirth: Morte, mother of the new life to come.

The thirteenth card (Death) signifies not only the transformation of our fear of death, but also points to another kind of death in the middle of life, a kind of death that the initiate will inevitably experience one day. The spiritual death of the ego makes the rebirth of the soul possible. People at this stage of evolution feel an initial death, which may be accompanied by the fear of loss and pain, and even a genuine danger to their continued physical existence. In any case, they must spend some time face to face with a higher existence; after undergoing this trial, they return to their "normal" lives stronger, more experienced and enriched. Many initiatory death rituals serve this same purpose. They are meant to free people from the fear of death, thereby making them ready for life. Goethe, too, recognized this when he wrote: "Until you have known this dying and becoming, you are but a gloomy guest on the dark earth." It is important to say "Yes" to Death as the great Changer and Transformer. When you say "Yes" to death, it means you are saying "Yes" to life.

The water sign Scorpio is the astrological sign of this card. In astrology, the scorpion is a creature that carries within it the mystery of transformation and death. The Hebrew letter of the card is NUN (fish). NUN embodies the emergence of life, including human life, from the water at the beginning of time and space in this world.

The rune of the thirteenth card is BERKANO, meaning "birch." BERKANO embodies the birch deity, the primordial mother who watches over the process of human and earthly metamorphosis, who guards birth, death and life, until the new resurrection and rebirth arrives. Death is no longer separate from life, just as life is no longer separate from death. All is one continuum; everything is a continuation of everything else. Krishnamurti clearly expresses the consequence of ignoring this connection when he says: "We have separated life from death, and the gap between the two is fear." We fear the changes that may come if we truly become ready to accept death.

title: Temperance
description:
"The virtuous man chooses the middle and avoids the two extremes of too much and too little."
Aristotle

After the death of the ego (the primary Death), which for many people is accompanied by a disturbance of the senses and a terrifying awareness, the initiate learns the lesson of balance. Only one who is in balance can safely use the energies that were released in the card of Death. It is not only mentally ill people, who spend their lives as patients in psychiatric hospitals, who are the victims of an inadequate understanding or misapplication of the power of Temperance.

Often people are so unruly and inattentive in their seeking that they push forward, grasping at sensations for which they do not yet possess the necessary maturity. This creates a kind of "short circuit" in their bodies. We must not forget that we are dealing here with very subtle, very high energies. Moreover, these energies are, above all, ready to work for humanity — our bodies and minds must be sufficiently mature and properly prepared for them.

Temperance, or perhaps better, Balance, is depicted in the Tarot of the Aquarian Age as a beautiful naked woman. The feather covering her nakedness signifies that she has shed so much of life's ballast that she has now become "light as a feather" and capable of flying like one.

Before her are placed two flat cups, containing a red and a blue liquid. These are the two energies, positive and negative, which have united in the middle in order to achieve balance and equilibrium. Although the young woman holds her hands above the cups, she does not actually touch them. This means she knows how to hold the subtle energies of polarity in her hands and is able to harmonize opposites through willpower alone.

Transformation is another theme of this card. Here it is depicted as the transformation of negative force into positive force. People who have reached this stage of evolution continue the task of transforming their negative qualities into positive ones, all the while remaining firmly anchored to their own center.

Card number fourteen is dedicated to the astrological sign of Sagittarius. He appears in the image of a centaur — half man, half animal — who hunts for his ideals. In one hand he holds a bow with the string drawn taut. Only when he overcomes his animal nature will his arrow be able to strike the target he has dreamed of for so long — the highest truth.

Sagittarius belongs to the element of fire, but water is also present in card number fourteen. The rune LAGUZ means cosmic, primal water. LAGUZ is also the gateway to that which is hidden. In this rune the depth of the soul is revealed in all its beauty, but also in all its ugliness. LAGUZ symbolizes a person's determination, willingly subjecting themselves to trials.

The Hebrew letter SAMEKH means "water serpent." The serpent coils itself into a closed ring, and the circle is completed. Humanity is born in water, under the sign of the fish (serpent). This sign is ideal for our plane of reality, since this is how God wished to see it, He who desired that they should strive for the perfection contained within Himself.

title: The Devil
description:
"The noble man loves virtue, the common man loves material gain. The noble man weighs the consequences of his actions, the common man thinks only of the profit he can gain from his deeds."
Confucius

After Temperance comes the Devil. This poor Devil once again plays the role of the Tempter. Now that the seeker has begun to feel the safety and balance he has achieved, he is confronted by the great Tempter, temptation in forms corresponding to the seeker's own abilities and inclinations. The Devil can wear a thousand faces. He can appear in the guise of an advantageous business deal, whose profit is achieved at another's expense. He can manifest himself as envy, laziness, greed, gluttony, vanity, pride, and finally as sexuality.

But why was the Devil chosen to play the role of the Tempter? The explanation is simple enough. He feeds on the shadow, the dark side of our being. He holds up a mirror before us, so that we may look into the most remote corners of our ego and understand who and how we truly are. The more we try to suppress or deny our negative qualities, the more they show themselves, and the harder they become to transform. The Devil, with all his temptations and traps, helps us become aware of our own negative manifestations.

For centuries, the concept of the "Devil" was strongly influenced by the figure of Pan, the Arcadian god of shepherds. Part man, part animal, with the horns and hooves of a goat, Pan plays his pipes and drives the nymphs into a state of terrible panic. (The word "panic" derives from Pan.) Like Pan, the Devil also delights in frightening people. Evidently, so long as the Devil can make a person tremble with fear and worry, that person is sure to forget the fact that she or he is a child of God.

What lies behind the figure of the Devil, or the god Pan? If God is truly all and everything, then there can be no place here for anyone but God. In this light the Devil is a manifestation of one aspect of God: God's opposite. In this role, the Devil is very important in the world of phenomena. While the divine energies help humanity ascend, the diabolical energies pull it back down again. Our task, in this phase of mutually contradicting energies, is to rise above the lower energies and reassess the significance of the Devil for humanity, so that he too may once again become a rightful part of the whole — restored to his true unity, but in a state of full awareness.

The Devil is the card of temptation on every plane, including that expression of sexuality which aims only to satisfy the lower instincts. As long as a person remains the victim of this instinctive compulsion, he remains the victim of the Devil. When a person awakens to higher consciousness, he will continue to enjoy sexuality, but will no longer be dependent on it.

Card number fifteen in the Tarot of the Aquarian Age depicts a young man surveying his surroundings through eyes that radiate an almost magnetic attraction. It is very hard for you to escape this irresistible gaze. He can read the thoughts of the person facing him, turning them to his own advantage, enriching both his own creativity and that of the person before him. He works with transformed energy at this phase of development. The Devil can, therefore, be a constructive and creative energy — if that energy is directed into the right channel.

The mechanical metal objects in the upper part of the card symbolize the potential danger of this diabolical energy. The more we mechanize our world, the further we move from our source, and the greater the danger that we will perish in cataclysms. Nature is patient, always ready to nourish and please humanity, but if people treat her cruelly, she will turn against them. The result will be a catastrophe that could end in the total destruction of the Earth. That is why every individual must work on themselves. Pollution of the outer environment is not only around us — it is within us. A radical change must occur at the very core of each individual, so that the surrounding environment too can be purified.

The astrological sign of this card is dedicated to the cardinal earth sign, Capricorn. The goat is endowed with persistence and endurance; it climbs the highest mountain peaks, almost inaccessible summits that cannot be reached without the greatest discipline. The Devil, too, possesses persistence and endurance, and he uses these qualities to lie in constant wait, ready to seize the chances contained within human weakness.

The Hebrew letter AYIN (eye) is found in the left corner of the card. With any eye you can perceive the same thing, regardless of which eye it is. But what kind of gaze is achieved here — only a superficial glance, or a penetrating one? If SAMEKH the serpent (the Devil) prevails in life, then only the outer eye functions, and a person sees only fragments of the truth. AYIN and ALEPH — the first letters of the Hebrew alphabet (which denote unity) — have more in common than you might suppose at first glance. ALEPH embodies God in His Unity; AYIN is the seeing eye. Could it also be the eye of God, an eye turned inward? When we reflect on this, it helps us grasp more deeply the interconnections that join God and the Devil.

The rune ELHAZ means "elk." This rune is considered one of the most powerful in Germanic symbolism. It also resembles an upraised hand with open fingers, a gesture whose deep meaning includes humanity and protection. ELHAZ symbolizes the vital energies and rebirth embodied in the mystical elk. In addition, ELHAZ signifies the transpersonal factor, one that looks upon interdependencies, protection from unwanted outside influence, the unmasking of illusions, and independence from external suggestion.

The energy directly responsible for leading people astray is the energy of the Devil. It would not be wise to try to destroy this energy. The wise allow this energy to serve them, transforming it in order to achieve noble goals.

title: The Tower
description:
"Now or never! I must seize this precious moment."
Friedrich Schiller

The gathered energy of the previous card (the Devil) has run out of control and caused destruction. The fortress has been struck and broken into two parts.

The Tower embodies the architecture of human thought. It is the structure we have built in order to hide within it. It is our ego and everything we have devised in order to protect that ego. In the French Tarot decks, this card bears the name La Maison de Dieu — the House of God.

Three builders worked to raise this Tower. The first is ignorance (that is, not knowing the fact, not knowing the fact that spiritual teachings must not be materialized, but belong to the spiritual sphere). The second builder is fanaticism, whose ego tries to shut the gates of the house of God and bar the entry of others, because: "I can do it better," "I know better," or "Others are not worthy." The third builder is ambition, arrogance, which wants to raise the highest Tower, pierce the heavens and reach God. In this light, each of us builds our own Tower of Babel, a structure in which we are at once prisoner and jailer, until lightning strikes, shaking and destroying our Tower — but, at the same time, setting us free.

The Tower symbolizes a society which, through its own arrogance and lack of wisdom, regards itself as the center of the universe and exploits it, taking into account its supposedly inherent right to exploit the planet. Until a fundamental reassessment takes place, human society should not be surprised if, one day, the annihilating lightning truly does strike, breaking everything in its path.

But the devastation depicted on this card also carries the seeds of healing. Those who have survived and lived through this phase of loss know that a material, intellectual or spiritual upheaval cannot destroy their deepest essence. They recognize God and His all-knowing freedom, and know that this intense experience, at this phase, has contributed to their spiritual maturation.

On the sixteenth card of the Tarot of the Aquarian Age you see the Tower, which looks destroyed, without any outward impulse. The door of the Tower is closed; communication with the outer world is no longer possible. Inside the Tower is a bright room, where spiritual energy has been gathered. Blocked energies, deprived of any outlet, lead to the dangerous situation depicted on this card: they must break their chains.

The floor of the bright room is paved with a checkerboard pattern of black and white squares. This alludes to two planes within human beings: the material plane (black) and the spiritual plane (white). People cannot overcome the division that separates them from the higher sphere until they transform the matter in which they live (that is, their own physical bodies). This transformation is necessary so that body and spirit can survive the shattering trial that this card symbolizes.

As might be expected, the astrological sign of this card is the planet Mars in its destructive, annihilating aspect as the God of War. But we must not forget that new construction will follow destruction. This time, the architecture of the Tower will express our deeper understanding of structures and foundations — or we may freely choose not to build another Tower at all.

The Hebrew letter of this card, PE, means "mouth" or "tongue." It is said to be "the mouth through which God speaks." We also know that "God spoke, and the word was created," and this word embodies the word spoken by God. But the words formed by a human mouth are likewise waiting to take shape. Whether a person thinks, weeps or laughs, and whether they wish it or not, everything they have ever thought or said will return to stand before them one day. Think thoughts of love and speak words of friendship, and you will render the greatest service to the planet. The power of destruction that befalls the Tower will pass us by without harm, and the planet will once again become what it once was — a corner of paradise.

The rune of the Tower is IR (yr), and its meaning is the opposite of what is denoted by the rune ELHAZ on the previous card. The vital energy in ELHAZ has become blocked energy in IR, and everything will keep exploding until change comes about through PE, the mouth.

title: The Star
description:
"Where clarity reigns, there is also calm, or calm gradually arises of its own accord."
Wilhelm von Humboldt

The individual who has left the destructive aspect of the Tower behind is free as the wind and can reach the stars. Everything is luminous and clear. Myriad spiritual beings draw near to support and accompany them. Life is so beautiful! Thank You, O Creator, who has accompanied us through all our accomplishments.

The attributes of this card are humanity, love, awareness, wisdom and a deep understanding for other people. The initiate on the plane of the Star says: "I have lived through temptation and been reborn from pain. Now God the Father-Mother is guiding me toward the resolution of new tasks."

Without You I am like a speck of dust on the wind. Without You I am a wild blossoming, dark waters. Without You I am a destroying flame. Without You I am a careless word that brings ruin. Thanks to You, O Lord, I have become a Star!

A tremendous capacity for surrender is needed before initiates can acknowledge all of this and gaze with equal delight upon both the path they have traveled and the path that still awaits them.

We have reached the point of retrospection. The first five cards embody the following philosophical principles: I. The Magician: I am not only body, but also spirit. II. The High Priestess: Polarity, the not-yet-revealed mystery, this world and the beyond, duality. III. The Empress: The feminine being in all her aspects, the Great Mother, nature. IV. The Emperor: The earthly father, the law of order, the protector, matter. V. The Priest: The spiritual father, the first steps toward surrender, love, two spiritual paths.

At this point the first moral trial has taken place. It is followed by these further lessons: VI. The Lovers: From this point onward, teachings are tested, decisions are made and physical love is known. VII. The Chariot: Decisions are made, mastery over one's own life. VIII. Strength: Energy transformed. IX. The Hermit: The desire for perfection. X. Wheel of Fortune: Control over one's own feelings and instincts, and the ability to turn the Wheel of one's own Fortune. XI. Justice: The fulfillment of the law of love for oneself and others. XII. The Hanged Man: The absolute surrender of the ego. XIII. Death: Sacrifice within oneself — change.

At this point in the process, having drawn upon their own accomplishments, initiates begin to recognize what is happening around and within them. XIV. Temperance: The attainment of balance, an art. XV. The Devil: The trial of confronting matter and sexuality. XVI. The Tower: One of the final trials of courage — the initiate must lose everything before he or she can attain everything. XVII. The Star: Receptivity, sensitivity, being guided, contact with the master. Here mystical illumination begins. XVIII. The Moon: Understanding of the subconscious, acceptance, further courageous progress. XIX. The Sun: The card of Thou and of harmony. XX. Judgement: Total awakening. XXI. The World: The consciousness of every individual soul in its connection to the absolute spirit. 0. The Fool: End — beginning — a new plane.

Card number seventeen of the Tarot of the Aquarian Age shows the profile of a young woman. Her face radiates a clear inner beauty. The expression on her face is gentle, yet resolute. Looking at her face, you can tell that she has transformed her selfish desires and her self-image into real deeds. In her crown chakra shines a sparkling light, her personal Star, the one guide she allows to lead her. Who is this woman? She is Eve, representing the whole embodiment of humanity. Having endured so many harsh trials, she has attained the highest illumination and lives an authentic life with real courage. She knows that everyone has their own destiny to fulfill, that everyone has taken on a mission. All embodied beings work, in part for themselves, on a program that must be carried out. Every journey on this Earth has been given a purpose, and the most significant step along the way has been set and determined. Confusion and pain always arise when a person strays from the path of destiny they have chosen for themselves. The freedom to decide can lead us far from our true path, but that same freedom can also reunite us with ourselves and our path.

Individuals at the stage of development symbolized by the Star can hear the voice of their master and will no longer stray from their true path. They feel purity, an impersonal love for themselves and others. They are fully on the way to becoming masters themselves.

The Hebrew letter is TZADI (hook). According to the Bible, we now live in the Age of Pisces. The hook will lead humanity into the coming Age of Aquarius. Card number seventeen is dedicated to the astrological sign of Aquarius, an air sign that embodies openness toward everything new.

The rune of the Star is EIHWAZ, meaning "yew." This rune denotes the vertical axis of the world tree. Everything created exists according to this defining principle. The yew is also the sacred tree of magicians and shamans. The deep purity presented in this card spreads joy and gives hope for a better world.

title: The Moon
description:
"In the depth of winter, I understood that an invincible sun dwells within me."
Albert Camus

Everything seems so clear, so obvious, and we feel so close to our goal in card number seventeen. In the card called "The Moon," however, everything once again becomes hazy, unclear, hidden. New obstacles arise to separate the seeker from their goal.

This card in the Tarot of the Aquarian Age depicts a young woman in a dreamy or meditative pose. She holds one hand before her face to shield herself from a beam of moonlight. In truth, though she is neither dreaming nor meditating, she is trying to remember. She examines the past and everything she has lived through. Every action, every thought is assigned its proper place. She does not evaluate or judge things, but simply experiences each thing once more before finally separating herself from it. Every human bond, every relationship she has entered into, dissolves itself in deep love. She knows that every trivial feeling will hinder her progress. She must reject every materialistic desire, she must free herself from every attachment, if she wishes to find and walk the unknown path lit by the moon.

On the left side of the card, a drawing reproduces the Moon as it is depicted in well-known Tarot decks: the face of the moon against the sun. We also see two towers on the horizon, right and left, and two howling dogs before them. At the edge is depicted a pond, on whose surface we see a creature resembling a crayfish. A narrow winding path curves between the pond, the dogs and the towers. The pond symbolizes the human subconscious, all the suppressed deeds and desires that we must now bring into the light, even if that light is nothing more than pale moonlight. The bottom of the pond reaches back toward the origin of humanity, a source that must be found in the past. Just as crayfish prefer to move backward, so too must people travel back through their past all the way to the source. The two dogs are the two human instincts — the instincts of self-preservation and of procreation — the same instincts we already encountered in card number ten (the Wheel of Fortune). We must not allow ourselves to be frightened by these two barking monsters (instincts). If the desire to reach our goal is truly strong enough, we will indeed develop further, and the dogs will not be able to scare us off or dissuade us.
